text: Lesson 24 built Patient Scheduling Application Service out of real CIs. This lesson closes the loop Chapter Three opened, decides where Discovery takes over maintaining those CIs, configures Identification Rules so Discovery doesn't duplicate what was just built, and checks all of it against the CMDB Health Dashboard.

The Technical Service gets mapped to its Business Service, Patient Scheduling, using CSDM's Technical Service to Business Service relationship. Without that mapping, a director asking what breaks if Patient Scheduling goes down has no path from the business-facing record down into the real infrastructure CIs from Lesson 24 — the chain breaks at the first step.

Going forward, Discovery maintains the infrastructure CIs: SCHED-APP-01, SCHED-APP-02, and SCHED-SQL-01. The application CI and the Business Service mapping stay manually governed, since Discovery knows what infrastructure exists, not what business service it supports. That requires a MID Server with real line of sight into Meridian's clinical-systems network segment, plus WinRM credentials for the servers and separate database credentials for SCHED-SQL-01.

Without the right Identification Rules, Discovery's first scan creates brand-new duplicate records instead of recognizing the three CIs already built by hand. The fix is identifying the servers by fully qualified domain name and serial number, and the database instance by instance name plus host server, so that first scan reconciles into the existing records instead of duplicating them.

The CMDB Health Dashboard is where this gets validated, not assumed. Completeness checks that all four CIs have their required attributes filled. Correctness checks that the duplicate count sits at zero. Compliance checks that every CI has its expected relationship. Currency checks that the Discovery-maintained CIs show a recent last-discovered timestamp instead of going stale.

A clean read across all four metrics is what turns this from records that were built once into records that can actually be trusted. Next: closing the capstone with a real governance plan — named ownership, a review cadence, and what to keep monitoring after this project ends.
